title: Pointer arithmetic and how arrays really work
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why p + 1 moves by the size of the type, why array indexing is pointer arithmetic in disguise, and where the boundary of defined behaviour sits.

blocks.text: Adding to a pointer does not add bytes. It moves by elements — the compiler multiplies by the size of the pointed-to type. Once that clicks, array indexing stops being a separate feature and becomes shorthand for something you already understand.

blocks.caption: The multiplication is implicit
lines: int *p = values;          /* an array name used in an expression becomes a pointer to its first element */
printf("%d\n", *(p + 1));  /* 20 — moved 4 bytes, because int is 4 bytes */
printf("%d\n", *(c + 1));  /* moved 1 byte — a different type, a different step */

blocks.title: a[i] is defined as *(a + i)
blocks.text: That is not an analogy — it is the definition in the standard. Which also means i[a] compiles and does the same thing, since addition commutes. Nobody writes that, but knowing why it works tells you that indexing and pointer arithmetic are one mechanism, not two.

blocks.text: The rule that keeps this defined

items: You may point at any element of an array, and at one position past the last element
That one-past-the-end pointer may be compared and used as a loop limit, but never dereferenced
Going further than one past the end is undefined — even computing the pointer, without reading it
Pointer arithmetic between unrelated allocations is undefined, even if the addresses look adjacent

blocks.caption: The boundary, precisely
lines: int *p = a + 4;      /* legal: one past the end — this is why loops can say q < a + 4 */
int *q = a + 5;      /* undefined behaviour, even though nothing is read */
printf("%d\n", *p);  /* undefined: reading the one-past-the-end position */

blocks.title: Off-by-one is the most common way this goes wrong
blocks.text: for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) reads one element past the end of an n-element array. In a language with bounds checking that is an exception; in C it reads whatever follows in memory. The same mistake in a write turns into memory corruption, and it is exactly the shape behind a great many buffer-overflow findings.

blocks.text: Viewing an object as a sequence of unsigned char is explicitly permitted, which is why memcpy, hashing, and serialisation all work through that type. It is also how you inspect what your data really looks like in memory — a technique the endianness lesson uses directly.

blocks.title: Prove that indexing is arithmetic
steps: Print v[2], *(p + 2), and 2[v] — confirm all three are 30
Print (void *)p and (void *)(p + 1) and note the difference is 4, not 1
Cast to char * and print the same two addresses — now the step is 1
Print (v + 3) - v and confirm it is 3, not 12
Write a loop that runs to i <= 4 by mistake and run it under -fsanitize=address
Read the report, then fix the condition
blocks.expected: Three spellings of the same element, addresses that step by the type size, a pointer difference measured in elements, and an off-by-one that the sanitizer catches at the exact line. That last one is the single most common defect in C, seen on purpose.

cheatsheet: p + 1 moves forward by sizeof(*p) bytes, not one byte
a[i] is defined as *(a + i) — indexing IS pointer arithmetic
An array name in an expression becomes a pointer to its first element
Subtracting two pointers gives a count of elements, not bytes
You may form a pointer one past the end, and compare it, but never dereference it
Two past the end is undefined even if you never read it
for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) is the classic off-by-one — it touches one element too many
void * has no type: you cannot dereference it or do arithmetic on it portably
unsigned char * is the correct type for examining raw bytes

checkpoint.prompt: int *p points at an array. How far does p + 1 move in bytes?

choices.C: It depends on the array length

checkpoint.explanation: Pointer arithmetic counts elements. The compiler multiplies by the size of the pointed-to type, which is why the type on the pointer matters.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the relationship between a[i] and *(a + i) ?

choices.A: They are similar but a[i] is safer
choices.B: They are the same thing — a[i] is defined as *(a + i) in the standard
choices.D: *(a + i) only works for the first element

checkpoint.explanation: Indexing is notation for pointer arithmetic. Neither form does any bounds checking.

checkpoint.prompt: For int a[4], which is allowed?

choices.A: Computing a + 5 as long as you never read it
choices.B: Computing a + 4 and comparing it, but not dereferencing it
choices.C: Dereferencing a + 4 to read the terminator
choices.D: Both a + 4 and a + 5, since neither is read

checkpoint.explanation: One past the end is a defined position precisely so loop conditions can use it. Two past is undefined even without a read.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can you not dereference a void * ?

choices.B: It carries no type, so there is no size to read and no interpretation to apply — assign it to a typed pointer first
choices.D: You can; the compiler infers the type

checkpoint.explanation: void * is the way C says 'an address to some data'. The type has to come from somewhere before the memory can be read.
